newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: COFFEE--Colombian growers in winter of discontent.
newsitem.headline: COFFEE--Colombian growers in winter of discontent.

text.p: The leader of an independent coffee growers' association said Wednesday that public apathy was the only thing likely to prevent strikes and potentially violent protests from erupting in Colombia's central coffee-growing region next year.

Fabio Trujillo, head of the National Coffee Growers' Union, said growers were grappling with their worst crisis in recent history thanks -- in part -- to soaring production costs, higher-than-expected inflation and last week's announcement of a cut in Colombia's internal coffee price.

But Trujillo, an outspoken critic of the powerful National Coffee Growers' Federation, said most cash-strapped growers were too busy trying to make ends meet, and make the next payment on high-interest loans, to think about rising up in protest against government economic policy and the government-affiliated Growers' Federation.

"There ought to be a strong outpouring of discontent, a march, a work stoppage, a strike or whatever. But I don't think it will happen ... Nobody is in a mood to do much of anything anymore," Trujillo said in a telephone interview from his family's plantation outside the central city of Manizales.
"The Federation has a capacity to dominate people. But no coffee grower can be content right now with what it's doing," Trujillo added.

The Federation has complained in strongly-worded statements since last summer that a rapidly strengthening peso was crippling the coffee sector because real export revenues have eroded steadily as the dollar becomes cheaper on local foreign exchange markets.

But Trujillo said the Federation, which held its annual convention last week, had failed to win any real commitment from the government to ease the foreign exchange crisis undermining Colombia's most important industry in terms of jobs and its second-largest source of export revenues.

"The only thing certain is that they (the Federation) lowered the coffee price on us. And that worsens even more -- if there's room for more -- the very serious situation Colombia's coffee growers are already in," Trujillo said.
"The results of the convention were absolutely negative," he added. "A very serious injustice was committed."

Trujillo, whose loosely-woven organization maintains a strong presence throughout most of Colombia's coffee-growing region, said he planned to hold talks with regional representatives on Jan. 20 to discuss the crisis that now looks set to worsen next year.
But he said there was little that he or other independent growers could do barring "a change from top to bottom" in the Growers' Federation.
"Colombian coffee policy has to undergo definitive changes, both externally and internally," he said.

He warned that unemployment was already skyrocketing in areas like central Caldas province, where his own coffee plantation is located, because an increasing number of growers were being forced out of business.

"A lot of people are abandoning their plantations," he said, adding that this explained a sharp drop in coffee output in some areas in 1996. "The people who stay do so because they're obliged to stay, they can't do anything else."
Trujillo said the growing impoverishment of Colombia's traditionally well-to-do coffee families threatened to trigger serious social unrest in areas like Caldas in the near future.
"It used to be a privilege to live here because nothing ever happened," he said of the once-tranquil village where his family has grown coffee for generations.
"But we're seeing a lot of robberies now, there's a lot of thefts and insecurity because of the unemployment stemming from the crisis in the coffee sector."
